passage:
It had been eight months since Layla told Xin the truth about the late nights at the studio in Vancouver: she had been meeting an ex, and lying about it.
She had been honest since. Home when she said. Phone left face-up on the counter. Answers before he asked.
And still, Xin caught himself watching. When her phone buzzed at dinner, his eyes went to it before he could stop them. When she said "work", some part of him paused, checking the word for cracks.
He was so tired of it. It felt like a background app draining a battery all day.
One Sunday in the market, she stepped away to take a call, and he kept choosing tomatoes. He didn't look up. Only later, walking home, did he notice he hadn't wondered who it was.
"What?" Layla asked, because he was smiling.
"Nothing," Xin said. "Something good."

qa.q: How long ago had Layla told Xin the truth?
qa.a: Layla had told Xin the truth eight months earlier.

qa.q: How did Xin feel about still watching for signs of lying?
qa.a: Xin felt exhausted by it, like an app draining a battery all day, and wished he could stop scanning her words.

qa.q: What small moment showed Xin that things were changing?
qa.a: At the market, when Layla took a call and Xin kept choosing tomatoes without wondering who it was, he noticed the watching had begun to ease.

qa.q: How might Layla experience Xin's months of watching?
qa.a: Layla may find it hard to be checked even while honest, but her steady behaviour is what slowly lets Xin relax.

grounding: Months after Layla's lie, Xin notices he still scans for signs of deceit and feels tired of it, until a small moment shows the watching easing.

passage:
The sample freezer logs at the research institute had to be checked every four hours. In January Simran had filled in two entries she hadn't actually checked, and a batch was nearly lost. She had owned it fully, in front of the whole lab.
Since then she hadn't missed a check.
But Pranav, who shared the night rota with her, still opened the freezer every time after she'd logged it. He didn't tell anyone. He just did it, quietly, and felt ashamed and exhausted in equal parts.
"You double-check me," Simran said one night in March, not angrily.
Pranav's ears went hot. "I know. I'm sorry. I can't seem to stop."
"It's all right. I'd probably do the same."
In May, he realised on the bus home that he had skipped the extra check twice that week without deciding to. The logs had matched every time.
He felt lighter, and a little surprised.

qa.q: How often did the freezer logs have to be checked?
qa.a: The freezer logs had to be checked every four hours.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel while double-checking Simran's work?
qa.a: Pranav felt ashamed and exhausted in equal parts, unable to stop watching for another false entry.

qa.q: What helped the checking ease for Pranav?
qa.a: Simran's honest logs matching every time for months, and her calm acceptance of his checking, let his watchfulness fade without forcing it.

qa.q: How might Simran feel knowing Pranav still checks her work?
qa.a: Simran seems to understand; she is not angry and says she would probably do the same, accepting it as part of repairing trust.

grounding: Pranav, hurt by Simran's past false logs, notices he still checks her work and is tired of it, and finds it eases as her honesty repeats.

passage:
In their small house near the church in Pala, Elizabeth caught herself doing it again. Anand came home at 6:40, and before he'd even put down his bag she had checked his shoes for mud, smelt his shirt, and glanced at the clock on the wall.
Eight months ago she had found out he'd been lying about the loan from his cousin, and about the Sunday afternoons "at the farm". He had told her everything since. He had shown her the repayment papers without being asked.
Still, her eyes kept scanning. She was so tired of it. It felt like being a guard in her own house.
That evening she told him, "I keep checking you. I hate it."
Anand sat down next to her. "Then check. I'd rather you check than wonder."
She laughed, a little wetly. The next week she noticed she had forgotten to look at the clock twice. Only twice. But it was something.

qa.q: What time did Anand come home?
How does Elizabeth feel about her own checking?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels tired and trapped by it, like a guard in her own house, and says she hates it.

qa.q: What helps the scanning ease over time?
qa.a: Anand's steady honesty, showing papers unasked and welcoming the checks, so each honest day makes watching a little less needed.

qa.q: How does Anand respond to being checked?
qa.a: Anand accepts it calmly, saying he'd rather Elizabeth check than wonder.

grounding: Shows a hurt wife noticing she still scans for signs of lying and is tired of it, and the scanning starting to ease as honesty repeats.

passage:
In their flat in Prague, Jana lay in bed at midnight, looking at Omar's "last seen" time on the chat app. 11:52. He had said goodnight at 11:30. Her chest tightened in the old familiar way.
Three months ago she had discovered the second account he'd used to message his ex for most of a year. He had deleted it in front of her, answered every question, and hadn't broken a single promise since.
And still she scanned. Last-seen times. Which way his phone lay on the table. Whether he smiled at a message.
She was exhausted by herself.
In the morning she asked, trying to sound casual, "You were online late?"
"My brother," Omar said, and turned the screen toward her without being asked. The message was about their mother's birthday cake.
Jana let out a breath. It was the ninth time something like this had turned out to be nothing. She was starting to count less.

qa.q: What time did Omar's 'last seen' show?
How does Jana feel about her own scanning?
qa.a: Jana feels exhausted by herself, chest tightening each time, even though Omar has kept every promise.

qa.q: What is slowly helping Jana count less?
qa.a: Omar answering openly and showing messages without being asked, so each check that turns out to be nothing eases the need to scan.

qa.q: How does Omar respond when asked about the late message?
qa.a: Omar treats it as part of repair, turning the screen round without being asked.

grounding: Shows a hurt partner tired of her own watching for lies, with the scanning beginning to ease as honest answers repeat.

passage:
At the community health centre, Binita reached for Yusuf's patient register again and stopped herself halfway.
In spring he had marked home visits as done when he hadn't made them. Two elderly patients had missed follow-ups. He had admitted it in front of the medical officer and taken a warning. Since then every register had been accurate. Every single one. She knew, because she had checked every single one.
Her colleague Mrudula noticed. "You're still re-counting his visits?"
"I can't stop," Binita said. "It's like a tap I can't turn off. I'm so tired."
"That's normal after what happened," Mrudula said. "It'll ease if he keeps being straight."
That Friday Binita checked only half of Yusuf's entries, picked at random. All correct. The next month, a quarter. She noticed her shoulders sitting a little lower.

qa.q: What had Yusuf marked as done in spring?
qa.a: He had marked home visits as done when he hadn't made them.

qa.q: How does Binita feel about re-checking Yusuf's registers?
qa.a: Binita feels tired and stuck, like a tap that won't turn off, even though every register has been accurate.

qa.q: What approach helped Binita ease the checking?
qa.a: Checking a smaller random sample each month, half and then a quarter, as Yusuf's accurate records kept repeating.

qa.q: How does Mrudula see Binita's checking?
qa.a: Mrudula sees it as normal after what happened and expects it to ease if Yusuf keeps being straight.

grounding: Shows a health worker still checking a colleague who once lied, tired of it, and the checking easing as honest records repeat.

passage:
Dear Yash,
It's been six months since you told me the truth about the shop accounts, and I want to be honest with you about something, the way you've been honest with me since.
I still check. When you say the supplier was paid, I look at the bank statement that night. When you're late back from the market, I notice I'm counting the minutes. When you laugh on the phone, part of me listens for what's behind it. I hate it. It's exhausting, and it makes me feel like a guard instead of a partner.
But I also notice something. Every statement I've checked has matched. Every late evening had a reason you'd already texted. The checking is getting shorter. Last week I forgot to look at all, and only remembered on Sunday.
So I'm not writing this to accuse you. I'm writing because I think this is a stage, and I'm in it, and it's easing because you keep showing up the same way.
Pradeep

qa.q: How long ago did Yash tell the truth about the shop accounts?
qa.a: Six months ago.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel about still checking?
qa.a: Pradeep feels exhausted and hates it, feeling like a guard instead of a partner.

qa.q: What is helping the checking ease?
qa.a: Yash's honest behaviour repeating: every statement matched and every late evening came with a text, so the checking is getting shorter.

qa.q: How might Yash feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Yash may feel a sting at being checked, but also relieved and encouraged that the steady honesty is working.

grounding: Shows a hurt person noticing they still watch for signs of lying and feel tired of it, and that the watching eases as honest behaviour repeats.
